request.query: QuantaCloud raises or cuts GPU prices

results.title: QuantaCloud GPU 怎么选？A100、H100、L40S 和按秒退款规则讲清楚 | 智机玄同
results.author: 智机玄同 发布于 2026年10月9日 3 分钟阅读
highlights:
QuantaCloud 提供按需 GPU VM，启动先预扣一小时，停止后退回未用秒数。本文解释 A100 SXM/PCIe、H100、L40S 的当前配置和数据删除规则。

智机玄同发布于 2026年10月9日 3 分钟阅读

资料核查日期： 2026年10月9日。价格、库存和服务商规则可能变化，请以官方页面为准。

文章目录

QuantaCloud 的计费方式有点特别。

它不是“每秒从余额里一点点扣”，而是：

启动时先扣一小时，停止时再把这一小时里没用掉的秒数退回来。

所以最终效果仍然是按实际运行秒数结算。

官方 FAQ 说得很清楚：跑 3 小时 17 分钟，最后就是付 3 小时 17 分钟。

## 当前公开单卡价格

截至 2026-10-09，QuantaCloud 当前 pricing catalog 里比较重要的单 GPU 配置包括：

- A100 PCIe 80GB：$1.48 / 小时
- A100 SXM4 80GB：$1.50 / 小时
- L40S 48GB：$1.09 / 小时
- H100 PCIe 80GB：$2.69 / 小时

这些不是单独一张 GPU 的裸价。

官方页面明确说明，小时价包含整台 VM 的 GPU、vCPU、RAM 和本地磁盘。

## A100 SXM4 单卡配置

当前一套 1× A100 SXM4 80GB 配置是：

- 16 vCPU
- 120GB RAM
- 1,000GB 本地磁盘
- us-midwest-1
- $1.50 / 小时

QuantaCloud 还有其他地区的 A100 SXM4 单卡配置。

本站结构化数据选取一套明确的 1× 配置，而不是拿 8× GPU 节点除以 8 来假装单卡实例。

现在可以直接进入：

## A100 PCIe 又有什么区别

当前一套 1× A100 PCIe 80GB：

- 16 vCPU
- 96GB RAM
- 768GB 本地磁盘
- us-midwest-2
- $1.48 / 小时

如果你只用单卡，SXM 和 PCIe 的区别未必会像多卡训练那么明显。

真正要多 GPU 通信时，SXM / NVLink 的价值才更容易体现。

可以同时看 A100 PCIe Compare。

## L40S 单卡是什么配置

当前一套 1× L40S：

- 12 vCPU
- 72GB RAM
- 625GB 本地磁盘
- $1.09 / 小时

48GB 显存卡里，它仍然很适合卡在 32GB 和 80GB 中间的任务。

## H100 PCIe 单卡

当前 pricing catalog 的 1× H100 PCIe：

- 20 vCPU
- 128GB RAM
- 1,250GB 本地磁盘
- $2.69 / 小时

这条会进入现有 H100 PCIe Compare。

## 最大的坑不是价格，而是磁盘

QuantaCloud 当前 On-Demand VM 有一条必须提前知道：

Stop 会终止 VM，并删除它的本地磁盘。

官方当前也说明没有持久卷和 Snapshot。

所以你不能像普通 VPS 那样随便关机，然后几天后回来继续。

模型、checkpoint、输出文件如果还要保留，停止以前要先复制出去。

这对训练任务尤其重要。

## 网络流量当前不另外收费

QuantaCloud 当前 pricing 页面说明：

- ingress 免费；
- egress 免费。

这对经常搬模型、数据集和结果的人比较友好。

但不要因此忽略本地磁盘删除风险。

网络免费和数据持久化是两件不同的事。

## 余额不足会怎样

QuantaCloud 使用预付余额。

如果余额不足以支付下一小时，官方说明实例会被终止，并删除磁盘。

所以跑长训练时，不只是“余额不足任务暂停”。

它有可能直接让本地数据一起消失。

长任务应该：

- 开 Auto top-up；
- 留足余额；
- 定期把 checkpoint 复制出去。

## QuantaCloud 更适合什么人

比较适合：

- 需要标准 Ubuntu GPU VM；
- 希望价格里已经包含 CPU / RAM / 本地盘；
- A100 / H100 / L40S 用户；
- 可以接受临时实例、自己管理数据备份；
- 希望 ingress / egress 规则简单。

如果你需要“停机后几天再原地恢复”，当前这种产品形态反而不适合。

results.title: GPU marketplaces vs managed clouds: Vast.ai, io.net, Clore vs Lambda · RentGPU
results.author: Vi Nguyen
highlights:
A marketplace does not own most of the hardware it lists. Independent hosts (small datacenters, hobbyists with a few cards, former crypto mining operations, companies with idle capacity) install the platform's agent, set a price, and the marketplace matches them with renters, takes a cut, and handles payment. The platform controls the software layer: the container runtime, the listing and search interface, billing, and usually some kind of host reputation system. It does not control the power supply, the cooling, the PCIe topology, the network uplink or who has physical access to the box.

A managed cloud buys or leases its own servers, puts them in datacenters it chooses, and runs them with its own staff. Everything below your container is its responsibility. When a GPU starts throwing errors, the provider replaces it. When the network is slow, it is the provider's problem to fix. You pay for that accountability in the hourly price.

...

The price difference follows from that. A host who already owns a card and pays for the electricity can accept any price above their marginal cost, and competition pushes listings toward that floor. A managed cloud has to recover datacenter leases, staff, spare inventory and support, and it has to price for the utilization it actually achieves.

## The price spread, live

The two tables below show current per-provider prices for a consumer card and a datacenter card. The RTX 4090 is where marketplaces dominate, because it is a consumer part that many small hosts own and relatively few managed clouds list. The A100 80GB is a datacenter part that both models sell, so it is a fairer head-to-head.

Nvidia GeForce RTX 4090 — live prices by provider

| Provider | Median $/hr | Range | Offers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| io.net | $0.30/hr | $0.30/hr–$0.30/hr | 8 |
| Novita AI | $0.33/hr | $0.33/hr–$0.33/hr | 11 |
| RunPod | $0.34/hr | $0.34/hr–$0.34/hr | 1 |
| Nosana | $0.36/hr | $0.29/hr–$0.70/hr | 7 |
| CloudGPU | $0.39/hr | $0.39/hr–$0.39/hr | 341 |
| Lium | $0.40/hr | $0.30/hr–$0.63/hr | 29 |
| Clore.ai | $0.46/hr | $0.27/hr–$1.67/hr | 71 |
| Vast.ai | $0.50/hr | $0.40/hr–$2.00/hr | 18 |

Live data, last 24 hours. Full Nvidia GeForce RTX 4090 page.

Nvidia A100 80GB PCIe — live prices by provider

| Provider | Median $/hr | Range | Offers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lium | $0.81/hr | $0.81/hr–$0.81/hr | 2 |
| Thunder Compute | $1.09/hr | $1.09/hr–$1.79/hr | 5 |
| Hyperstack | $1.35/hr | $1.35/hr–$1.40/hr | 2 |
| QuantaCloud | $1.48/hr | $1.48/hr–$1.48/hr | 1 |
| CloudGPU | $1.59/hr | $1.59/hr–$1.59/hr | 8 |
| Ukiyo | $1.64/hr | $1.64/hr–$1.64/hr | 1 |
| Cyfuture AI | $2.10/hr | $2.04/hr–$2.10/hr | 4 |
| Sesterce | $2.20/hr | $2.20/hr–$2.86/hr | 2 |

Live data, last 24 hours. Full Nvidia A100 80GB PCIe page.

Look at two things. First, the median gap between the cheapest marketplace and the managed providers on the same card: that is the premium you are being asked to pay for operated infrastructure. Second, the width of each marketplace's own range: a wide range means host quality varies a lot, and the cheapest offer is often cheap for a reason. The cheapest listing anywhere right now is $0.81/hr on Lium for the A100 80GB and $0.30/hr on io.net for the RTX 4090.

...

On a managed cloud, a single host failure is rare and, when it happens, the provider owns the fix. On a marketplace, reliability is a property of the individual host, and it ranges from excellent to terrible. Consumer machines in homes can lose power, get rebooted for a driver update, or drop offline when the owner's internet does. Hosts can also delist a machine or raise its price. None of this is malicious; it is what happens when capacity comes from many independent operators. The practical effect is that any job longer than a few hours on a marketplace should be checkpointed as if it were running on spot capacity, even when you paid for on-demand. The math for that is in our spot vs on-demand guide.

results.title: RTX A6000 48GB 云 GPU 怎么选？从 $0.35 到 $1.89 的整机价格差在哪 | 智机玄同
results.author: 智机玄同 发布于 2026年10月10日 2 分钟阅读
highlights:
RTX A6000 48GB 已有多家公开云实例可比。本文比较 Thunder、Beam、QuantaCloud、Runpod、Paperspace 的配置与计费。

智机玄同发布于 2026年10月10日 2 分钟阅读

资料核查日期： 2026年10月10日。价格、库存和服务商规则可能变化，请以官方页面为准。

文章目录

RTX A6000 是一张很实用的 48GB Ampere 专业 GPU。它没有 L40/L40S 的 FP8，也不是 A100 的 HBM，但 48GB 显存、ECC 和成熟 CUDA 生态让它仍然适合视觉生成、视频、3D 和中等规模推理。

## 当前公开价

截至 2026-10-10，满足本站完整比较门槛的单卡公开价：

- Thunder Compute：$0.35/小时
- Beam： from $0.54/小时
- QuantaCloud：$0.55/小时
- Runpod Secure Cloud：$0.59/小时
- Paperspace：$1.89/小时

完整配置见 RTX A6000 48GB Compare。

## 为什么价格差这么大

同一张 GPU 不等于同一台机器。Thunder 的 CPU/RAM 可调，Beam 把 8 vCPU、64GB RAM、500GB NVMe 打进机器价，QuantaCloud 是 6 vCPU、24GB RAM、256GB 本地盘，Runpod 是 Pod 形态，Paperspace 则是传统 Machine。

如果任务主要吃 GPU，低价平台很有吸引力；如果工作流吃系统内存、需要持久环境或现成生态，就要把周边资源一起算。

...

A6000、L40、L40S 都是 48GB，但代际不同。A6000 属于 Ampere；L40/L40S 属于 Ada，支持 FP8，视频和推理能力也更现代。

如果只是“需要 48GB 显存”，A6000 往往能用更低租价解决问题。需要更高推理吞吐、视频编解码或 Ada 特性时，再看 L40/L40S。

results.title: The Cheapest H100 Is Out of Stock: What 25 Clouds of GPU Pricing Data Shows | beCloudReady
results.author: Chandan Kumar
highlights:
On 14 October 2026 the lowest H100 price in our tracker was $1.66 per GPU-hour, listed by Latitude. That row is marked out of stock. The cheapest H100 that a provider says you can rent right now is $3.30 per GPU-hour, at Scaleway. That is almost double.

This is the problem with most GPU price comparisons: they rank list prices and stop. A list price you cannot rent is not the best price. This post explains what we changed in our open GPU price tracker, what the data shows today, and where it cannot tell you the answer.

...

After this week's changes, the 14 October snapshot has:

- 518 priced offers across 25 providers (up from 436 offers and 18 providers before the change)
- Hyperscalers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle) and GPU-specialist clouds in the same table
- A per-GPU-hour price, so an 8-GPU node and a single-GPU instance compare fairly

...

Stock data comes from the marketplace source only. AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle, RunPod, Lambda, Nebius and the other direct sources publish prices but no stock. Of 518 offers, 51 are in stock, 158 are out of stock and 309 are unknown.

...

## What the data shows on 14 October

Median per-GPU-hour price of the offers in the tracker (not matched by instance size, so read these as a market snapshot rather than a benchmark):

| GPU | Offers | Providers | Lowest listed | Median | Highest listed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | 50 | 17 | $1.66 (Latitude, out of stock) | $3.25 | $10.00 (Oracle) |
| H200 | 21 | 10 | $2.25 (Excess Supply, out of stock) | $5.29 | $10.60 (Azure) |
| B200 | 17 | 9 | $3.74 (BoostRun, out of stock) | $7.79 | $14.24 (AWS) |
| A100 80GB | 45 | 14 | $1.35 (Excess Supply, in stock) | $1.98 | $4.10 (Azure) |
| L40S | 46 | 12 | $0.69 (BoostRun, out of stock) | $1.70 | $7.58 (AWS) |

Three things stand out.

1. The cheapest listing is usually not rentable. For H100, H200, B200 and L40S the lowest listed price is marked out of stock. For H100, 27 of the 50 offers are out of stock, 3 are in stock and 20 are unknown. A ranking that ignores this tells you to go to a provider that has nothing to sell you.

2. Hyperscalers cost about twice as much at the median. The median H100 offer is $5.75 per GPU-hour on the four hyperscalers and $2.73 on everyone else. For A100 80GB it is $3.55 against $1.52. Some of that gap is real capacity guarantees, networking and enterprise terms. Some of it is simply price. Whether the gap is worth paying is a decision about your workload, and a price table cannot make it for you.

3. The spread within one GPU is wide. The highest H100 listing is six times the lowest. If your team defaults to one cloud for every job, you are probably paying the top of that range for work that does not need it.

...

- Unknown stock is not available stock. For H100, 20 of 50 offers have no stock data. The cheapest in-stock H100 we can verify is $3.30, but a direct provider with no stock signal could be cheaper and rentable.
- Marketplace prices can include a markup. Shadeform resells capacity from other clouds. A marketplace price may differ from the same provider's own price page, and the marketplace may list a provider that also appears elsewhere.
- On-demand only. Spot, reserved and committed-use prices are excluded. They can change the ranking.
- Stock changes within hours. The snapshot is nightly. Treat it as where to look first, not as a reservation.
- Per-GPU price is not total cost. Egress, storage, minimum commitments and setup time are not in the number.

results.title: Is GPU compute tight? The answer is in contract length | SecondSource
highlights:
CoreWeave, a cloud company that specializes in renting out GPUs, the chips AI runs on, says rental prices rose about 25% starting in July. Yet a public index that the website getdeploying compiles from the list prices on dozens of providers' websites read only a 5% rise over a year in mid-September. Both numbers can be right. Almost all of CoreWeave's revenue comes from customers on contracts, while the index collects only the hourly, stop-any-time prices listed on websites (pay-as-you-go), so the two numbers measure different prices. Where compute is visibly tight, with more would-be renters than machines, is contract length: customers who sign for only three to six months pay 2.5 to 4 times the price of a five-to-six-year contract. That is above the gap of about 2 times between renting by the hour and signing for three years in the public market (SecondSource's conversion), but the two multiples cover different terms, so the gap can only be called high. No multiple calculated the same way exists for earlier years, so how much tighter than in past years cannot be said. Long contracts also require 20% to 30% up front. In October, after another provider raised list prices, the index's one-year rise reached 18%. CoreWeave's third-quarter results will show how fast new prices lift the average price across all of CoreWeave's contracts.

...

In the same period, the getdeploying public index read only a 3.3% rise over four weeks and 5% over a year for the week of September 14. SecondSource's September 18 daily brief drew a conclusion from the gap: the tightness is concentrated in newly signed short-term contracts, out of sight of public prices.

...

CoreWeave's second-quarter 10-Q says 98% of revenue comes from committed contracts and only about 2% from pay-as-you-go. CoreWeave's pricing page lists the H100, one of NVIDIA's GPU models, at US$6.16 per GPU per hour, the figure read on October 18. The site keeps no older versions, so whether this price moved around July can't be checked. In the public index, CoreWeave also appears at US$6.16.

So the 25% most likely went into the prices of new and renewed contracts: even if the listed price did move, the change would touch only about 2% of revenue. The CFO did not say which kind of price the 25% refers to; this reading rests on the 10-Q and the pricing page. The two numbers also cover different periods, so the two cannot be compared directly: the 25% is one company's single price change in July, and the 5% is a year's rise in dozens of providers' listed prices.

...

## Six: In October, another company's listed prices moved

For the week of October 12, getdeploying's reading became 9% over four weeks and 18% over a year; SecondSource's recomputation from getdeploying's public weekly data matches. In the same period Nebius, another GPU rental company, raised listed prices from October 1 (Nebius pricing page). The H100 went from US$3.85 to US$4.50 an hour, and the increases across the H100 and three other NVIDIA GPU models, the H200, B200 and B300, ranged from 17% to 21%.

So the public index can see price increases; what the index sees are increases in listed prices. The index is calculated by GPU model, and in the week of October 12, 21 of 26 models rose; getdeploying hasn't broken out which providers changed prices or how much each contributed.

...

Details of the public index. Each week getdeploying records every provider's pay-as-you-go listed price. getdeploying takes a median for each provider and then a median across providers, one vote per provider, leaving out reserved and spot prices. SecondSource recomputed October 12 against September 14 from getdeploying's public weekly data: the median change across the 26 models is 8.6%, and against October 13, 2025 it is 18.2%. Nebius's new prices from October 1 were reported by the press by September 17 (Investing.com): the H100 from US$3.85 to US$4.50, the H200 from US$4.50 to US$5.40, the B200 from US$7.15 to US$8.50 and the B300 from US$7.85 to US$9.50. Several outlets called it the second increase in three months. All five data-center models in the index rose between September 14 and October 12: the H100 from US$3.34 to US$3.51, the H200 from US$4.44 to US$4.86, the B200 from US$6.52 to US$7.99, the B300 from US$7.87 to US$8.99 and the A100 from US$1.75 to US$1.82. The rise is uneven across generations: the H100 is up 5% over four weeks, the B200 up 23%. Compute Desk, another index provider, builds its index from completed transactions. Compute Desk says the B300 pay-as-you-go price rose 17 days in a row to a record on October 15, at about US$7 to US$10 an hour, about 64% above November 2025. That account comes from a single secondhand source. The September 18 call also said that a near-double-digit quarterly rise in the public index in the fourth quarter would mean the two measures had converged. A 9% rise over four weeks is already close, but what rose is the listed price itself.

results.title: Neocloud pricing climbs while AI inference costs fall — TechReaderDaily
results.author: M Mireille Otsuka Staff reporting
highlights: The upward leg is not subtle. Nebius raised major GPU prices 17% to 21%, and short-duration capacity negotiations have reached $40 million to $50 million per megawatt, per Seeking Alpha's September analysis. CoreWeave signed new compute capacity contracts at higher prices in the third quarter of 2026, adding $25 billion in commitments. Set those against the Vera Rubin roadmap and you have a three-year contract written at 2026 prices for hardware that will produce tokens at a fraction of 2026 cost. That is a good trade for a seller with a backlog and a bad trade for a buyer who signed without a price-reset clause.

results.title: Why GPU prices spike during AI compute shortages | CloudPe Blog
results.author: Gautami Teliwadekar
highlights:
GPU prices spike when AI demand outpaces the memory, chip packaging, and power new GPUs need. In 2026, NVIDIA’s RTX PRO 6000 list price rose from $8,565 to $16,000, and B200 rentals jumped 79% in three months. Yet H100 rentals fell 64% to 75% from their 2024 peak.

...

A GPU price spike is a sharp rise in what buyers pay to rent or own a GPU, usually within weeks or months. It shows up in two places: hourly cloud rates and hardware list prices. The two can move at different times and by different amounts.

Contract type matters too. Spot and on-demand rates track the market daily, while reserved contracts lock a price for a year or more. In 2026, reserved H100 prices rose about 40% while on-demand prices fell, because on-demand capacity was sold out.

## GPU prices in 2026

Cloud GPU rental prices are up 13% over 12 months across 21 models, with 16 rising and 5 falling. The GPU prices chart below shows the biggest moves. Rental figures are in US dollars per GPU-hour.

| GPU or price type | Earlier | Latest | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100, one-year contract | $1.70 (Oct 2025) | $2.35 (Mar 2026) | +38% |
| H100, on-demand median | 12 months ago | $3.57 (week of 12 Oct 2026) | +19% |
| B200 rental | 3 months ago | $8.01 (Sept 2026) | +79% |
| RTX PRO 6000 list price | $8,565 (Mar 2025) | $16,000 (Aug 2026) | +87% |

Note: Trackers measure different things, so the same GPU can show different prices. On 7 October, one list-price median put the H100 at $4.20, while trade-based indexes showed about $2.81 to $2.86.

...

GPU prices spike because demand rises fast while supply cannot. New supply depends on memory, packaging, and power that take quarters or years to expand. With supply fixed, price absorbs the extra demand.

Three forces stack up. Demand jumps when new AI products launch. Supply is capped by a few scarce parts. Contracts then lock capacity away, so less reaches the open market. Prices rise first where capacity is tightest: newest GPUs, high-memory cards and reserved contracts.

...

GPU prices spike when new demand lands before new supply, and they fall when supply catches up.

...

| Period | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Early 2024 | H100 rentals peak at $8 to $10 an hour |
| Dec 2025 to Jan 2026 | H100 on-demand up 10% in four weeks, from $2.00 to $2.20 |
| Mar 2026 | One-year H100 contracts reach $2.35 |
| Jun 2026 | H100 eases to $2.01 to $2.53 as Blackwell supply ramps |
| 1 Oct 2026 | Nebius raises H100 on-demand from $3.85 to $4.50 |

results.title: LITEON and QCT Showcase NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 ...
results.author: Irene Chou, Chizuru lizuka
highlights:
LITEON Technology (2301.tw) and Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), a leading provider of data center and AI solutions, jointly showcased an AI rack-level infrastructure solution supporting the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform at the 2026 OCP Global Summit. The demonstration features LITEON's 110kW Power Shelf integrated within a rack-level power architecture, highlighting how advanced power delivery and system integration can support the growing token-processing requirements driven by agent ... AI while improving computing performance and energy efficiency for ... factories.

...

LITEON showcases its 110kW Power Shelf designed to support NVIDIA MGX architecture. Delivering high power density within a compact footprint, the solution provides the rack-level power required by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems while maximizing space available for compute resources. Equipped with high-efficiency power conversion, intelligent load balancing, and digital power management capabilities, the solution is designed to accommodate rapid power fluctuations associated with AI training, inference, and Agentic AI workloads, ensuring reliable operation while reducing energy loss and thermal burden. Combined with QCT's expertise in AI platforms, system design, and data center integration, the two companies are working closely on platform-level co-design and validation to help customers accelerate deployment of high-density AI infrastructure built on the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform.
